<FromTheBinary topic="auth integration" />

Your users sign in to your application, not to Cyoda. Your application decides
what each user may do, then calls Cyoda for them, and Cyoda records each
change for the user and for the client that made it. This page walks through
what to create, what to send and what comes back. The model behind it is in
[Authentication and identity](/concepts/authentication-and-identity/).
Endpoint and setting details are in
[Identity and IAM](/reference/identity-and-iam/).

The examples use the tenant `acme` and the host `cyoda.example.com`. The
responses were captured from a cyoda-go server in JWT mode. Tokens and
secrets are shortened.

## The parts of an application

| Part | Client | Grant | A change is recorded as (for / by) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Backend acting for signed-in users | On-behalf-of | Token exchange | the user / the backend's client |
| Background job or script | Plain, one per job | `client_credentials` | the client / the client |
| Compute-node service | Plain, one per service | `client_credentials` | the transaction's origin / the node's client |
| Tenant admin | Admin, or the operator per change | `client_credentials` | the admin client / the admin client |

**Use one client per part.** A part is one deployable unit with one job. All
replicas of a part share its client, and separate parts never share one. Each
part can then be rotated or revoked on its own, and the executor recorded on
every change names the part that made it.

There is no finer permission split. Every plain or admin client holds
`ROLE_M2M`, which reaches every data operation of the tenant, and any plain
client can join as a compute node. Treat every client secret as access to all
of the tenant's data.

## Step 1: get a tenant and its first admin client

**Who:** the platform operator, once per tenant.

A tenant exists as soon as a token names it, and only the operator's
`cyoda token` can name a new one. Run it where `CYODA_JWT_SIGNING_KEY` is
available, then create the tenant's first admin client. The node that takes
the call must run with `CYODA_IAM_M2M_ADMIN_ROLE_ENABLED=true`.

```bash
# Kubernetes: kubectl exec POD -- /cyoda token --tenant acme
ADMIN_TOKEN=$(cyoda token --tenant acme)

# -H @- reads the header from stdin, which other local users cannot see.
curl -X POST "https://cyoda.example.com/api/clients?clientId=acme-admin&withAdminRole=true" \
  -H @- <<<"Authorization: Bearer ${ADMIN_TOKEN}"
```

Hand the `client_id`, the `client_secret` and the tenant id to the tenant
admin over a secure channel. A standing admin client is the most powerful
credential of the tenant. The alternative is to have the operator sign a
short-lived `cyoda token --tenant acme` for each administrative change.

## Step 2: create one client per part

**Who:** the tenant admin.

```bash
# A token for the tenant admin: HTTP Basic, credentials on stdin.
TENANT_ADMIN_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://cyoda.example.com/api/tenants/acme/oauth/token \
  -K- <<<"user = \"${ADMIN_CLIENT_ID}:${ADMIN_CLIENT_SECRET}\"" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "grant_type=client_credentials" | jq -r .access_token)

# The backend's on-behalf-of client.
curl -X POST "https://cyoda.example.com/api/clients?clientId=backend-obo&onBehalfOf=true" \
  -H @- <<<"Authorization: Bearer ${TENANT_ADMIN_TOKEN}"

# One plain client per compute-node service and per job.
curl -X POST "https://cyoda.example.com/api/clients?clientId=billing-job" \
  -H @- <<<"Authorization: Bearer ${TENANT_ADMIN_TOKEN}"
```

```json
{
  "client_id": "backend-obo",
  "client_secret": "de95…d548",
  "client_secret_expires_at": 0,
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange",
  "onBehalfOf": true,
  "roles": ["ROLE_M2M"]
}
```

The secret is shown once. Store each `client_id` and `client_secret` in your
secret store at once, under a name that says which part uses it. That store
is your inventory. A re-run that creates an id the tenant already holds gets
`409 M2M_CLIENT_EXISTS`. If the store has no secret for that id, reset the
secret with `PUT /clients/{clientId}/secret` rather than delete and create
again.

Your application must know its tenant id from configuration: the credentials
response does not carry it.

## Step 3: register the application's trusted key

**Who:** the tenant admin. Every node must run with
`CYODA_IAM_TRUSTED_KEY_REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true`.

Generate the key pair where the backend runs. The private key never leaves
it.

```bash
openssl genrsa -out app-key.pem 2048

# The JWK modulus n, base64url without padding. The exponent 65537 is "AQAB".
N=$(openssl rsa -in app-key.pem -noout -modulus | cut -d= -f2 \
    | xxd -r -p | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')

curl -X POST https://cyoda.example.com/api/oauth/keys/trusted \
  -H @- -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"keyId\":\"backend-key-2026-11\",\"jwk\":{\"kty\":\"RSA\",\"n\":\"${N}\",\"e\":\"AQAB\",\"alg\":\"RS256\",\"use\":\"sig\"}}" \
  <<<"Authorization: Bearer ${TENANT_ADMIN_TOKEN}"
```

`GET /oauth/keys/trusted` then lists it:

```json
[
  {
    "active": true,
    "jwk": { "alg": "RS256", "e": "AQAB", "kid": "backend-key-2026-11", "kty": "RSA", "n": "xZyEjnejDeuM…", "use": "sig" },
    "keyId": "backend-key-2026-11",
    "legalEntityId": "acme",
    "validFrom": "2026-11-22T22:05:38.889098Z",
    "validTo": "2027-11-22T22:05:38.889098Z"
  }
]
```

The `keyId` becomes the `kid` your backend signs with. Without `validTo`, the
key is valid for 365 days; rotate it before then (see [Rotation](#rotation)).

## Step 4: act for a signed-in user

**Who:** your backend, with its on-behalf-of client. Do this only after your
application has authenticated the user and decided that the user may do what
they ask. Cyoda applies the client's roles, never the user's.

<SequenceFlow label="Calling Cyoda for a signed-in user">

1. **User → Your backend** Signs in through your identity provider and makes a request
2. **Your backend → Cyoda** Token exchange: the on-behalf-of client's credentials plus a user assertion signed with the tenant's trusted key
3. **Cyoda → Your backend** Access token for the user, carrying the client's roles and naming the client in `act`
4. **Your backend → Cyoda** API call with that token
5. **Cyoda → Your backend** Response; the change is recorded for the user and executed by the client
6. **Your backend → User** Response

</SequenceFlow>

**Sign a user assertion.** It is a JWT with:

- header `"alg": "RS256"` and `"kid": "<keyId>"`;
- `sub`: your application's stable id for the user, 1 to 255 characters,
  recorded byte for byte (`Alice` and `alice` are two users). `system` is
  reserved;
- `caas_org_id`: your tenant id;
- `aud`: Cyoda's issuer, `CYODA_JWT_ISSUER` (default `cyoda`);
- `iat`: now, and `exp`: at most `iat + 300`.

Cyoda allows 30 seconds of clock skew and ignores every other claim, roles
included. It keeps no record of used assertions, so sign a fresh one for each
exchange and never let it leave your backend.

**Exchange it** at the token endpoint, authenticating the client with HTTP
Basic:

```bash
curl -X POST https://cyoda.example.com/api/tenants/acme/oauth/token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange" \
  -d "subject_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt" \
  -K- <<EOF
user = "${OBO_CLIENT_ID}:${OBO_CLIENT_SECRET}"
data = "subject_token=${USER_ASSERTION}"
EOF
```

```json
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs…",
  "expires_in": 300,
  "issued_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt",
  "token_type": "Bearer"
}
```

The issued token is for the user, acting through your client. Its payload:

```json
{
  "act": { "sub": "backend-obo" },
  "caas_org_id": "acme",
  "caas_tier": "unlimited",
  "caas_user_id": "alice",
  "exp": 1795385449,
  "iat": 1795385149,
  "iss": "cyoda",
  "jti": "a158c731-379c-47a8-ac4c-fa9f98fc6015",
  "scopes": ["ROLE_M2M"],
  "sub": "alice"
}
```

**Call Cyoda with it** as `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on HTTP, or
as gRPC metadata `authorization`. The token works on data operations only. It
never administers and never opens a compute-node stream.

**Cache one token per user.** Reuse the token until less than 60 seconds of
its life remain, then exchange a new assertion. Exchange once more if a call
answers `401`. The token lives until the assertion's `exp` at most, so sign
each assertion just before the exchange, with `exp = iat + 300`.

A backend in Node.js 18 or later needs no library for this:

```js
import { createPrivateKey, sign } from 'node:crypto';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const CYODA = 'https://cyoda.example.com/api';
const TENANT = 'acme';
const KEY_ID = 'backend-key-2026-11';
const privateKey = createPrivateKey(readFileSync(process.env.CYODA_TRUSTED_KEY_FILE));
const basic = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(
  `${process.env.CYODA_CLIENT_ID}:${process.env.CYODA_CLIENT_SECRET}`).toString('base64');
const b64url = (obj) => Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(obj)).toString('base64url');

function userAssertion(userId) {
  const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000);
  const input = b64url({ alg: 'RS256', kid: KEY_ID }) + '.' + b64url({
    sub: userId, caas_org_id: TENANT, aud: 'cyoda', iat: now, exp: now + 300,
  });
  return `${input}.${sign('sha256', Buffer.from(input), privateKey).toString('base64url')}`;
}

const cache = new Map(); // userId -> { token, expiresAt }

export async function tokenFor(userId) {
  const hit = cache.get(userId);
  if (hit && hit.expiresAt - Date.now() > 60_000) return hit.token;
  const res = await fetch(`${CYODA}/tenants/${TENANT}/oauth/token`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { Authorization: basic, 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
    body: new URLSearchParams({
      grant_type: 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange',
      subject_token_type: 'urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt',
      subject_token: userAssertion(userId),
    }),
  });
  const body = await res.json();
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`token exchange ${res.status}: ${body.error_description}`);
  cache.set(userId, { token: body.access_token, expiresAt: Date.now() + body.expires_in * 1000 });
  return body.access_token;
}
```

Each client may make `CYODA_IAM_TOKEN_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE` token requests per
minute on each node (600 by default). With 300-second tokens renewed when 60
seconds remain, one on-behalf-of client sustains about 2400 concurrently
active users per node.

## Step 5: work for no user

**Who:** background jobs, scripts and migrations. Each uses a plain client:

```bash
curl -X POST https://cyoda.example.com/api/tenants/acme/oauth/token \
  -K- <<<"user = \"${CLIENT_ID}:${CLIENT_SECRET}\"" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "grant_type=client_credentials"
```

```json
{"access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs…","expires_in":300,"token_type":"Bearer"}
```

Changes are recorded with the client as both the principal they are for and
the executor. Cache the token and fetch a new one when less than 60 seconds
remain. Never use an on-behalf-of token for work no user asked for.

## Step 6: connect a compute node

**Who:** each compute-node service, with a plain client that all its replicas
share.

1. Get a token with `client_credentials`. Only a client's own
   `client_credentials` token opens a stream. An on-behalf-of token or a
   `cyoda token` is refused with `PermissionDenied`.
2. Open the stream on the gRPC port with metadata
   `authorization: Bearer <token>`, and join with your tags and your tenant
   id as `joinedLegalEntityId`.
3. Keep the stream. It outlives the token that opened it. Cyoda re-reads your
   client every 60 seconds and closes the stream if the client was deleted or
   its secret reset.
4. For each callback into Cyoda, send the client's current token. Echo the
   callout's transaction token (`X-Tx-Token` on HTTP, `tx-token` on gRPC) when
   the callback must join the callout's transaction.

Reconnect handling for each stream status is on
[client compute nodes](/build/client-compute-nodes/) and in
[`cyoda help grpc`](/help/grpc/).

## What Cyoda records

Every change records the principal it is for and the executor. After the
exchange above, an entity created with alice's token shows in
`GET /entity/{entityId}/changes` as:

```json
[
  {
    "attributedKind": "user",
    "changeType": "CREATE",
    "executedBy": { "id": "backend-obo", "kind": "service" },
    "timeOfChange": "2026-11-22T22:05:59.465314Z",
    "transactionId": "e627744c-e6c0-11f1-8f45-ae468cd3ed16",
    "user": "alice"
  }
]
```

Audit events carry the same pair as `actor` and `executedBy`. Every callout
to a compute node carries it as `authtype`/`authid` (who the work is for) and
`authexectype`/`authexecid` (who does it). `authclaims` holds the executor's
roles, never the user's.

<Aside type="caution" title="Segregation of duties needs both principals">
`authtype == "user"` alone does not mean the user acted now. It is also true
for a compute node's write-back inside the user's transaction and for a
scheduled firing the user armed. An approval check requires
`authtype == "user"`, requires `authexectype == "service"` with `authexecid`
on an allow-list of your backend's on-behalf-of client ids, and compares
`authid` with the recorded submitter byte for byte. The full pattern is in
[`cyoda help auth integration`](/help/auth/integration/).
</Aside>

## Errors

The token endpoint answers in the OAuth error shape,
`{"error": "…", "error_description": "…"}`, and a retry is always safe:

- `400 invalid_request` with `subject token claims rejected` or
  `subject token has expired`: often clock drift or a stale assertion. Sign a
  fresh one and retry once. If it fails again, check `aud`, `exp − iat` and
  your clocks.
- Any other `400`, and `403 access_denied`: your request or setup is wrong.
  Fix it; do not retry.
- `401 invalid_client`: wrong credentials, or the client was deleted or reset.
  Re-read the secret store once, then stop and alert.
- `429 slow_down` and `503 temporarily_unavailable`: wait `Retry-After`
  seconds and retry, with backoff.

On data calls, a `401` did nothing: fetch a new token and send the same
request again, once. A second `401` with a fresh token is a configuration
error. A `403` is not retryable: use the right client. The full error tables,
with every `error_description`, are in
[`cyoda help auth integration`](/help/auth/integration/) and
[`cyoda help auth tokens`](/help/auth/tokens/).

## Rotation

- **A client secret, without downtime.** A reset ends the old secret at once.
  To rotate without a gap, create a second client of the same kind, roll every
  replica onto it, then delete the old client. If you keep an allow-list of
  `authexecid` values, add the new id first and remove the old one last.
- **A trusted key.** Register the new key under a new `keyId` while the old one
  stays active, and switch the backend to sign with it. After 300 seconds, no
  assertion signed with the old key can still be in flight; invalidate or
  delete it then. Tokens already issued are signed by Cyoda and stay valid.

If a private key or a secret leaks, invalidate the key or reset the secret at
once instead. The incident procedures are in
[`cyoda help auth integration`](/help/auth/integration/).

## Running it locally

Mock mode (`CYODA_IAM_MODE=mock`, the default) accepts every request as one
fixed principal and has no client store. The token endpoint and the client
endpoints answer `501`, so **on-behalf-of access cannot be exercised in mock
mode**. To run the flow above on one machine, start cyoda-go in JWT mode with
a signing key and trusted-key registration enabled:

```bash
openssl genrsa -out signing.pem 2048
CYODA_IAM_MODE=jwt CYODA_JWT_SIGNING_KEY_FILE=$PWD/signing.pem \
CYODA_IAM_TRUSTED_KEY_REGISTRATION_ENABLED=true \
CYODA_IAM_M2M_ADMIN_ROLE_ENABLED=true cyoda
```

Then `cyoda token --tenant acme --roles ROLE_ADMIN,ROLE_M2M`, in the same
environment, gives you a token that can create clients and keys and reach
data. The memory backend keeps nothing across a restart: clients and trusted
keys must be created again. The complete script, including signing the
assertion with `openssl`, is under *Running it locally* in
[`cyoda help auth integration`](/help/auth/integration/).

## Security checklist

- **TLS.** cyoda-go's listeners serve plaintext. Terminate TLS at the gateway,
  ingress or service mesh, and have every client and compute node verify the
  server certificate. A compute node can trust the callout attributes only
  over TLS.
- **Keep credentials on the server.** The trusted key's private key, client
  secrets, user assertions and Cyoda tokens never reach a browser or a mobile
  app.
- **Authorize before you act.** Cyoda records the user you assert and enforces
  only the client's roles.
- **Rate-limit the token endpoint** per source at the ingress (see
  [Identity and IAM](/reference/identity-and-iam/#token-endpoint)).
